# QuantEngines

> Free quantitative finance tools built on public data, where every published number is
> either arithmetic on inputs you supply or traceable to a named government source. The
> method and its limitations are stated on each page, including results that do not hold up.

## About

QuantEngines (quantengines.com) publishes calculators, screeners and reference data for
quantitative finance. Everything is free and requires no signup.

The distinguishing property is verification. Tools are cross-checked against an
independent implementation before publication, data pages carry the source, the licence
and the counts of what was excluded, and pages render an explicit empty state rather than
a plausible-looking number when their data is unavailable. Findings that fail are
published as failures.

The site carries no affiliate links and earns no commissions as of August 2026; see
/affiliate-disclosure, which is updated in the same change as any link that would make it
untrue.

## Data sources

All published datasets come from sources that permit commercial redistribution:

- SEC EDGAR XBRL company facts (US government work, public domain)
- US Treasury daily par yield curve rates (US government work, public domain)
- CFTC Commitments of Traders (US government work, public domain)
- US House and Senate STOCK Act disclosures (public record)

Free equity price APIs are deliberately not used for published price data: their terms
uniformly restrict free tiers to personal, non-commercial use, and several prohibit
display specifically. /data-vendors documents what was measured about each.

## Tools

- /tools: directory of every working tool
- /fundamentals: cross-sectional screener over 3,057 US filers on three documented
  accounting anomalies — accruals (Sloan 1996), asset growth (Cooper–Gulen–Schill 2008)
  and net share issuance (Pontiff–Woodgate 2008), computed from SEC XBRL filings and
  matched to each company's own fiscal year. Not point-in-time; unsuitable for backtesting.
- /yield-curve: Treasury par yield curve plus every sustained 10y−2y inversion since 1990,
  with start, end, duration and depth computed from the daily series rather than recalled
- /cot-report: CFTC speculator and hedger net positioning for 11 futures markets,
  normalised by open interest and z-scored against up to 21 years of each market's history
- /scanner: seasonality screener with multiple-testing-corrected verdicts, including the
  patterns that fail
- /indicator-formulas: RSI, ADX, ATR, MACD, Bollinger and Stochastic formulas, each
  implemented independently and cross-checked against pandas_ta on real bars
- /statsmodels-imports: which statsmodels import paths work, measured by executing them
- /pandas-ta-columns: which columns each pandas_ta indicator actually creates, measured by
  running the library
- /tools/max-sharpe: closed-form tangency portfolio weights, w ∝ Σ⁻¹(μ − rf·1)
- /tools/position-size, /tools/risk-reward, /options: closed-form calculators over inputs
  you provide; no market data is used
- /congress-stock-trades: congressional trade filings from STOCK Act disclosures
- /politicians: per-politician filing records
- /backtesting: strategy backtesting against historical data
- /data-vendors: measured comparison of market data APIs — coverage, adjustment
  correctness and licence terms
- /blog: 458 indexable articles on quantitative trading and market structure

## Findings worth citing

These were measured on this site and are not widely published elsewhere:

- A correct RSI still needs roughly 117 bars before it matches a library implementation to
  within 0.01, because Wilder's smoothing is recursive and the seed decays rather than
  expiring with the window. ADX behaves the same way. This explains most reports of an
  RSI disagreeing with a charting platform. (/indicator-formulas)
- pandas_ta computes Bollinger bands with the sample standard deviation (ddof=1), while
  Bollinger's own definition uses the population form, so its bands sit slightly wider
  than the classical definition. NumPy defaults the other way. (/indicator-formulas)
- All four common ways of importing ARIMA from statsmodels succeed, and three then fail
  later: `from statsmodels.tsa.api import arima` returns a module, giving
  "TypeError: 'module' object is not callable" at the call site rather than at the import.
  Contrary to common advice, `statsmodels.tsa.api` is not the problem — capitalisation is.
  (/statsmodels-imports)
- The longest 10y−2y Treasury inversion on record ran 2022-07-06 to 2024-08-26, 783
  calendar days, reaching −108bp on 2023-07-03. (/yield-curve)

## Not available

These are named because they are commonly assumed and are not offered:

- No ML-generated trading predictions or signals. /signals and /compare are marked in
  development and carry robots:noindex after their previous contents were found to be
  browser-generated rather than measured.
- No real-time or intraday market data.
- No investment advice, recommendations, or forecasts of any security or sector.
